the cAMP-elevated drugs inhibit the enhancement of intracellular Ca(2+) concentration and actin filament polymerization induced by fMet-Leue-Phe, and that the cAMP-dependent protein kinases are involved in the inhibition.
the cAMP-elevated drugs inhibit both Ca2+ release and actin polymerzation, which are induced by chemotactic peptide, in guinea pig peritoneal macrophaes.
intracellular cAMP may be involved in regulation of macrophage motility through inhibition of actin polymerizing activity and Ca2+ effluence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the cAMP-elevated drugs on the migration of guinea pig peritoneal macro phages stimulated with f-Met-Leu-Phe and the mechanism of action of the cAMP.
the effect of cAMP-elevation drugs on Ca2+-efflux and actin-polymerization in macrophage stimulated with N-formlyl chemotactic peptide.
the effects of intracellular c AMP on the migration of macrophages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the inhibition of migration by cAMP-elevated drugs may be due, at least in part, to the inhibition of Ca(2+)-dependent actin polymerization.
the cAMP-elevated drugs may inhibit macrophage migration by inhibiting the Ca2+ signal and actin polymerizations.
cAMP-elevated agents inhibited the actin polymerizing activity of macrophages and that the actin polymerized by fMet-LeU-Phe was depolymerized by cAMP-elevate agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the inhibition of actin polymeriztion is a major cause of the inhibition of macro-phage migration induced by the increase of intracelluar cAMP level, and that the increase of the monomeric G-actin content may be a cause of actin polymerzation.
cAMP-elevated macrophages are in the resting state and the migration of macrophages is induced by the decrease of cAMP level.
